title: Feedback from a 5-round controlled run (Claude Opus / Claude Code): blank WebGL captures, judge cause-attribution, non-reproducible FPS gate
body:
Ran dream-loop end to end with **Claude Opus 5 in Claude Code** (the README notes it's only been tested with GPT-6 Astra in Codex, so this may be useful coverage). Five controlled rounds against a fixed target, one variable per round.

**Results:** 1.55 → 3.50 → 4.45 → 5.65 → 5.42 / 10

| Round | Score | Δ | Single variable changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.55 | — | first pass |
| 2 | 3.50 | +1.95 | rebuilt from the judge's gap list |
| 3 | 4.45 | +0.95 | **parameters only** (13 values, zero geometry) |
| 4 | 5.65 | +1.20 | **geometry only** (the judge's own 5-item plan) |
| 5 | 5.42 | −0.23 | **medium only** (painterly post-process) — reverted |

The loop works. Scores were monotonic until the deliberate negative-result round, the judge had real discriminating power, and the stall rule fired twice at the right moments. Three things tripped me up that I think are fixable in the skill itself.

---

### 1. `/__capture` returns a blank PNG for any WebGL project

`scripts/preview-server.py` expects the page to POST its own canvas PNG, but a WebGL canvas defaults to `preserveDrawingBuffer: false`, so `canvas.toBlob()` after the frame has been presented returns an empty buffer. My first capture was a fully transparent 29 KB PNG and I nearly judged it.

Fix is one word in the consumer's code:

```js
new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ preserveDrawingBuffer: true })
```

Suggest noting this in the workflow docs next to the capture step, since 3D scenes are the skill's primary use case and every one of them will hit it.

### 2. The judge is reliably right about symptoms and unreliably right about causes

Round 1 the judge reported "no fog", "no bloom", "no tone mapping". All three were present and working — just too weak to read. It also reported the camera elevation as 50–55° when it was 27.9° (the real defect was shallow terrace relief), and told me to shrink the brick module to ~26px while its own measurements put my bricks at 22px.

Acting on its *prescriptions* was consistently right. Acting on its *diagnoses* sent me the wrong way.

I added one paragraph to the judge prompt and the behaviour changed immediately:

> Before claiming a rendering feature is "missing" or "absent", check whether it is present but too weak or occluded, and state which. Describe what you SEE; when you propose a cause, mark it explicitly as a hypothesis.

From round 2 onward the judge started verifying before asserting ("fog, bloom and tone mapping are all genuinely present — I verified with a gamma-lift pass") and explicitly retracted its round-1 claims. Happy to open a PR adding this to both workflow docs' judge prompt.

### 3. The FPS exit criterion isn't reproducible across sessions

`score >= 8 and target FPS acceptable` treats FPS as a stable property. After reverting round 5 I re-measured the *identical* build and got 44–50 fps where round 4 had measured 60 — the only difference was machine load from concurrent subagents. Same code, opposite sides of the gate.

If the criterion is meant to gate exit, it probably needs a fixed measurement condition, or a frame-time percentile over a stated window rather than an instantaneous average.

---

### One more, offered as an observation rather than a bug

The judge measures, and then prescribes optimising what it measured. In round 3 it diagnosed the terrain as too repetitive and backed it with a floor autocorrelation figure. I drove that number down by half in round 4 — and the image got worse. Its own round-4 write-up:

> This is my clearest error of the round. I diagnosed *repetition* and measured it with autocorrelation; the builder dutifully drove that metric down by half — and the picture got worse, because the real problem is *scale and hierarchy*, not repetition. **I was optimising a metric that was not measuring the defect.**

Worth a line in the judge prompt telling it to check that a proposed metric actually captures the defect before prescribing a target for it — a measuring judge can hand the builder a Goodhart trap, and the builder will comply.

---

Also worth knowing: the judge has no notion of scale truth. It compares pixels, so an archway built at 6 m instead of 3 m scores the same. I had orthographic spec sheets with metre dimensions for this project and used them as a second input alongside the target image; that combination worked well and might be worth mentioning as an option in `assets-3d.md`.

Thanks for putting this out — the stall rule in particular is the best-specified "when to stop iterating" heuristic I've seen in an agent skill, and it earned its place twice in five rounds. Glad to PR any of the above if useful.

title: Asked Muse AI To Update
body:
# Asked Muse AI:

> How can skill.md be improved

Applied on Version including Judge


# Got the following response:


First, an honest flag: I only found one other saved skill, not two. In ~/workspace/skills/ there's just dream-loop and reverse-engineer-web. Your uploads folder only has those two zips too (plus a skill-template.md, which is a blank template, not a skill). So either the second skill lives somewhere else, or you've got a third zip to send me. Point me at it and I'll review it the same way.

Now, dream-loop. It's a strong skill — the judge ladder and the stall/stalled exit logic are genuinely well-designed. But it has real gaps:

It never names the final deliverable. Same disease the reverse-engineer skill had. It says the loop ends at "score >= 8" — and then what? A folder? A zip? Where does the built game/app actually go, and how does the user receive it? Right now "done" is just a screenshot and a question. Concrete example: the loop finishes a beautiful browser game, but nothing says to package it with launchers or hand the user something they can double-click. Fix: add a final "Deliver" step naming the output format and handoff.

No pre-flight check. The skill lets you generate concept art, get user confirmation, then discover mid-build-loop that you can't take screenshots or spawn a judge subagent — there's a buried line saying "flag that to the user early and stop," but by then you've already burned their time and raised expectations. Fix: verify your tools before the concept art step — image generation? screenshot capture? subagents? Blender? List what's missing up front.

It never confirms the target platform. It hardcodes "60 fps for a browser game, 120 fps for mobile" and never asks what the thing runs on. A Quest 3 build, a Windows desktop app, and a web page are completely different jobs — different perf budgets, different screenshot methods, different delivery. Fix: confirm platform + minimum hardware alongside the target concept, and set the FPS bar from that.

It judges beauty, never "does it work." The ladder goes shape → light → materials → detail — but there's no gate for "the game actually runs without errors" or "the buttons do something." You could score a 9 on a screenshot of a build that crashes on click. Fix: add a Tier 0 "it runs" gate before the beauty judging starts.

Reverting is allowed but state is never saved. The exit criteria say "only revert if the score dropped by a full point" — but the skill never tells the builder to snapshot the build each round, so there's often nothing to revert to. Fix: one line — commit or snapshot the build at the start of every round.

The user is a spectator, not a participant. The only human moments are "confirm the concept art" and the final "want more iterations?" — with no guidance on how to present the concept (plain words? what will it feel like to use?). For a process that can burn a lot of tokens, the user deserves a plain-language picture of what they're buying before the loop starts. Fix: when presenting concept art, describe in everyday words what the user will see and experience, with a concrete example.

Want me to draft these as an addition to the dream-loop SKILL.md — a file for you to review before anything gets inserted?

title: fix(preview-server): add CORS preflight headers and /__status endpoint
body:
## Summary

Improves `scripts/preview-server.py` when the preview UI or capture harness runs on a separate local port/origin:

- **CORS + `OPTIONS` preflight**: Sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type`, and handles `do_OPTIONS()` with `204 No Content` so `POST /__capture` requests with `Content-Type: application/json` are not blocked by browser CORS preflight checks.
- **`GET /__status` health probe**: Exposes a lightweight JSON status endpoint reporting `has_target`, `has_latest`, and `latest_bytes` for `.dream-loop` capture verification.

## Verification
- Verified with `python3 -m py_compile scripts/preview-server.py` and HTTP `OPTIONS`/`GET /__status` checks.
